claims.text: Dynamic mechanical behavior in high-entropy alloys is governed by grain-boundary-mediated nucleation of partial dislocations under rapid loading.
Local chemical heterogeneities at grain boundaries enhance partial-dislocation nucleation.
Grain-boundary-mediated partial-dislocation nucleation causes plasticity to begin at lower strain than in single-crystal counterparts.
Polycrystalline HEAs have a higher initial work-hardening rate than single-crystal counterparts because of grain-boundary-mediated dislocation nucleation.
Grain boundaries are preferential nucleation sites for partial dislocations that grow into the crystal and leave stacking faults.
Under high-strain-rate loading, heterogeneous grain-boundary chemistry lowers the energy barrier for partial-dislocation nucleation.
Partial-dislocation nucleation produces an early accumulation of stacking faults in polycrystalline HEAs.
Interactions between stacking faults and dislocations impede dislocation motion and increase strain hardening.
Stacking-fault-mediated work hardening helps balance strength and ductility.
Single-crystal HEAs require higher strains to nucleate dislocations than otherwise comparable bicrystalline or polycrystalline HEAs.
Single-crystal HEAs exhibit delayed and more gradual work-hardening behavior relative to polycrystalline HEAs.
Under high-strain-rate loading, polycrystalline HEAs will exhibit lower yield strain and a steeper initial work-hardening rate than composition-matched single crystals.
Dynamically loaded polycrystalline HEAs will show earlier grain-boundary partial-dislocation nucleation and a higher stacking-fault density than single-crystal HEAs.
The proposed behavior should hold for equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEAs at moderate-to-high strain rates and ambient or moderately elevated temperatures where thermal recovery is not dominant.
Extreme grain refinement, annealing-induced changes in grain-boundary chemistry, or temperatures enabling extensive dynamic recovery may invalidate the proposed behavior.
Grain-size distribution and local composition can affect the magnitude of the mechanical response.
